The family list changes its wording at Jesus' birth

The list says about forty times that a man “became the father of” a son. Verse 16 breaks that pattern. Joseph is called the husband of Mary. Jesus is then said to be born “from whom,” meaning from her. Matthew does not say Joseph fathered him. Verses 18–25 explain the change. The four women named earlier also entered the line in unexpected ways.
The child's escape exposes the ruler's violence

Foreigners travel far to honor the child. The king of the land plans to kill him. Verse 13 saves the child by a warning and a night journey. Verse 16 shows that other children were not spared. Matthew does not explain that or soften it. He quotes Rachel weeping for her children (verse 18). The escape is told beside the grief of Bethlehem.
John demands changed conduct before inherited status

John addresses religious leaders in verses 7–10. Verse 8 demands fruit, meaning conduct that shows a changed life. Verse 9 names the claim they might use: descent from Abraham. John says God can raise children for Abraham from stones. Ancestry gives no protection. The ax is already at the root of the trees (verse 10). Being baptized is not enough without the change it stands for.
Scripture becomes a dispute over how the Son should act

In the second test the devil quotes Psalm 91:11–12. Both speakers are now using Scripture. Verse 7 answers with “Again, it is written.” Jesus sets one text beside another. Quoting a verse does not settle how to act. The devil uses a promise as a reason to force God’s hand. Jesus reads it within the command not to test God (Deuteronomy 6:16).
Repaired relationships belong before the offering

Verses 21–22 trace murder back to anger and insult. Verses 23–24 then give a case. A person stands at the altar with an offering. He remembers that a brother has something against him. The verse does not ask who was at fault. He must leave the gift and go to be reconciled first. Worship waits for the repaired relationship.
Hidden worship and divided service test the same heart

The chapter names two rivals for the heart. Verses 1–18 concern the wish to be admired. Verses 19–24 concern stored wealth. Verse 24 says a person cannot serve God and Mammon. Mammon means wealth treated as a master. Each rival offers a reward now: praise or security. Verses 25–34 follow with the worry that comes from serving wealth.
Hearing becomes secure only through action

The sermon ends with two builders. Both hear the same words (verses 24 and 26). Both build a house, and the same storm strikes both. Only one thing separates them. The first “does” what he heard, and the second does not. Hearing, agreeing, and admiring are not the foundation. Verses 21–23 have just warned that saying “Lord” is not enough.
Authority brings healing but does not guarantee welcome

The officer explains his request by describing his own work. He lives under orders, and he gives them (verse 9). A word from him is enough to move soldiers. He reasons that Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness. Jesus need not come to the house. Verse 10 says Jesus found no such faith in Israel. The chapter ends with a town that asks him to go (verse 34).
Mercy challenges the boundaries around a shared meal

The Pharisees object to the company at the table (verse 11). Verse 12 answers with a doctor, who goes where the sick are. Verse 13 then sends the critics back to Scripture. They should learn Hosea 6:6: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.” Their care for purity has left out mercy. Jesus says he came to call sinners. The meal is the cure at work.
The sent disciples depend on those who receive them

Verse 8 tells the twelve to heal and to charge nothing. They received freely, so they give freely. Verses 9–10 then take away their supplies. They carry no money, bag, or spare coat. They must depend on the households that take them in. The plan ties the messengers to their hosts. Verses 40–42 say that welcoming them counts as welcoming Jesus.
John's question meets evidence of healing rather than a title alone

John asks a direct question in verse 3. Jesus does not answer with a title. Verse 5 lists what is happening. The blind see, the lame walk, and the poor hear good news. The list echoes Isaiah 35:5–6 and 61:1. John is left to draw the conclusion from the evidence. Verse 6 adds a blessing for anyone who does not stumble over him.
Mercy answers accusations while the conflict becomes dangerous

Verse 1 gives the reason for the disciples’ act: they were hungry. Jesus answers from Scripture with David’s hunger (verses 3–4). Verse 7 quotes Hosea 6:6 again, as in 9:13. Mercy matters more than the rule as his critics apply it. He calls the disciples “guiltless.” The dispute then grows dangerous. Verse 14 says the Pharisees began to plan his death.
The field stories examine hearing, growth, and premature judgment

In the second story servants find weeds among the wheat. They offer to pull them out (verse 28). Verse 29 gives the owner’s reason for refusing. Pulling the weeds now would uproot wheat as well. The two look alike while they grow. Sorting belongs to the harvest and to the reapers (verse 30). The story warns against judging who belongs before the time.
Two meals reveal sharply different uses of power

The chapter sets two meals side by side. Herod’s feast is for the powerful. Verse 9 says he was grieved and still gave the order. His oath and his guests mattered more to him than a life. The meal ends with a head on a platter. Jesus’s meal is in a deserted place for hungry crowds (verses 15–21). It ends with everyone fed and food left over.
The woman's reply presses against the stated boundary

Jesus says it is not right to give the children’s bread to dogs (verse 26). She does not reject the picture. Verse 27 works inside it. Even the dogs eat what falls from the table. She asks only for crumbs. Verse 28 calls her faith great, and her daughter is healed. A foreign woman’s answer presses past a stated limit.
Peter recognizes Jesus but rejects the suffering he announces

Peter gives the right answer in verse 16 and is blessed for it. In verse 22 he tells Jesus that suffering must never happen. Verse 23 uses the harshest words in the chapter for the same man. Peter is thinking in human terms. He knows who Jesus is and rejects the path Jesus names. Knowing the title is not the same as accepting what it means. Verses 24–25 apply that path to every follower.
The mountain's glory does not remove the coming suffering

The voice in verse 5 repeats the words spoken at Jesus’s baptism (3:17). It adds a command: “Listen to him.” What he has just said is that he must suffer (16:21). On the way down he speaks of it again (verses 9 and 12). Verses 22–23 repeat it once more, and the disciples grieve. The glory on the mountain does not cancel that path. It tells them to trust the one who walks it.
Care for the small and mercy for debtors answer the rank question

The first servant owed ten thousand talents, a sum no one could repay (verse 24). The second owed a hundred denarii, a few months’ wages (verse 28). The king forgave the larger debt entirely. Verse 33 asks the question the story turns on. Should the forgiven man not have shown the same mercy? Forgiveness received was meant to change how he treated others. The chapter began with a question about rank and ends here.
Possessions expose the cost hidden inside the young man's question

The young man asks what he still lacks (verse 20). Verse 21 answers with one demand and one invitation. He should sell his goods, give to the poor, and follow. Verse 22 says he left sad, since he owned much. His sadness shows where the cost lay. He had kept the rules and could not let go of his wealth. Verse 26 says such a change is possible only with God.
Equal pay and serving challenge the pursuit of rank

The first workers received exactly what they agreed to (verse 13). No one cheated them. Verse 12 states their real complaint. The owner made the latecomers “equal to us.” They resent another’s gain, not their own loss. The owner asks whether his generosity makes them envious (verse 15). The request for the best seats shows the same concern for rank (verses 20–21).
The vineyard accusation names its immediate hearers

The vineyard story uses a picture from Isaiah 5:1–7. In it the tenants refuse to give the owner his fruit. Verse 45 says who understood themselves to be the target. The chief priests and the Pharisees saw that he meant them. The charge is aimed at those leaders in that place. Verse 46 shows the crowds on the other side, holding Jesus to be a prophet. The story should not be read as a charge against a whole people.
Tests about taxes and resurrection lead to love as the law's center

The lawyer asks for one great commandment (verse 36). Jesus gives two and joins them. The first is from Deuteronomy 6:5, and the second from Leviticus 19:18. Verse 40 says all the law and the prophets “depend” on these. The word pictures something hanging from a peg. Every other command hangs from love of God and neighbor. They are the measure for reading the rest.
The accusation examines burdens, display, and neglected justice

Verse 23 gives an example of careful obedience. These teachers tithe even garden herbs. Jesus does not tell them to stop. He says they “ought to have done” the weightier things as well. Those are justice, mercy, and faith. Small duties have crowded out large ones. Verse 37 shows that the speech ends in grief over the city.
Readiness means faithful care during an uncertain wait

The disciples ask for a date and a sign (verse 3). Verse 36 says the day is unknown. Verses 45–51 then describe what readiness looks like. A servant is set over the household to give them food on time. The faithful one is found doing that when his master returns. The bad servant beats the others and gets drunk. Being ready means caring for people during the wait.
The waiting stories end with care for people in need

Both groups in the last scene are surprised. The first asks when they saw the King hungry or in prison (verses 37–39). The second asks the same question (verse 44). Neither knew who was in front of them. Verse 40 gives the King’s explanation. What was done for the least of his brothers was done for him. The chapter’s stories of waiting end with care for people in need.
Jesus' arrest reveals failed promises and rejected force

A crowd comes with swords and clubs (verse 47). One of Jesus’s companions draws a sword and strikes (verse 51). Verse 52 tells him to put it away. Those who take the sword will die by it. Jesus says he could call on legions of angels (verse 53). He refuses force from his own side as well. Verse 56 then says all the disciples left him and fled.
The governor's handwashing does not stop his order

Pilate’s wife warns him that Jesus is righteous (verse 19). Pilate himself sees that envy lies behind the charge (verse 18). In verse 24 he washes his hands in front of the crowd. Verse 26 then reports what he does. He has Jesus flogged and hands him over to be crucified. The order is his. A public gesture does not undo the act that follows it.
The final promise sends uncertain disciples beyond the earlier boundary

Verse 17 says the eleven worshiped and that some doubted. Jesus sends them anyway. In 10:5–6 he sent them only to Israel. Verse 19 now sends them to all nations. Verse 20 closes the book with a promise: “I am with you always.” The book opened with the name Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23). The promise that began it also ends it.
